wrong: *-> include, import, incld - additional, include
right: *-> import - import library, an actual linked artifact
rule: a concept carries one mark; two marks on one head is a contradiction
why: the table filed U+2283 under include and U+2282 under incld, so the word could not be resolved without guessing. A wrong mark is worse than no mark: it makes a model act on a meaning nobody declared

wrong: *-> unknown, none, unk - unknown, unknown state of required param
right: *-> none - explicit absence of a value; *-> unknown, unk - not-yet-known
rule: a concept carries one mark; absence and unknown are two concepts
why: none is U+2204 and unk is U+2042. The embedding of 'none' is absence, so the pairing was not a synonymy - it was two meanings filed under one head

wrong: *-> graphics, render, visual, vis, UI  +  *-> vis, UI - visual element or type
right: *-> graphics, render, visual, UI - UI user interface mapping commands
rule: a word belongs to one concept
why: the second row owned no mark and every one of its words was already served by graphics, so it contributed ambiguity and nothing else
check: master: no word in two concepts

wrong: *-> map, mapping - logical map/dictionary
right: *-> map - logical map/dictionary
rule: one word per concept; a derivation is not a second word
why: mapping is the gerund of map. Two words for one thing is how a reader starts choosing between them
check: master: mapping absent from any head

wrong: *-> insert,       - logical action insert of any entity
right: *-> insert      - logical action insert of any entity
rule: the head must not promise an alias that is not there
why: a trailing comma reads as 'and here is another synonym'. Harmless to a reader who has the dictionary in context, a false signal to a fresh one - the only reader the base is written for
check: master: no trailing comma in a head

wrong: *-> any, ... - any operator of anything; ... is the spread form for lists over 10
right: *-> any - any operator of anything. `...` is NOT a name: spread notation, stays text, never compiles
rule: punctuation beside a word must be that word's ASCII form
why: RX_WORD only matches a leading letter, so `...` could never compile. The dictionary promised the model something the tokenizer cannot produce - worse than saying nothing

wrong: crt, chk, wrt, ret, req, rsn, src, swt, tab, len, sys, dir, synt, stat, excpt, exm, var, env, unk, targ, endp, vld, uniq, thm, uper, fun, func, par, proc, rm, mem, mk, locat, lst, inx, fmt, fin, fbd, cch, cos, crit, control, depend, lower, allw, answ, apr, arc, arch, bhvr, brk, bsns, cnv, conf, descr, els, err, evt, examp, extn, frmwrk, isol, landscp, reqred, respn, rvw, skl, svc, varn
right: create, check, write, return, request, reason, source, switch, table, length, system, directory, syntax, static, exception, example, variable, environment, unknown, target, endpoint, valid, unique, theme, upercase, function, param, procedure, remove, memory, make, location, list, index, format, finally, forbidden, catch, cosine, critical, controller, dependency, lowercase, allow, answer, approve, architecture, behavior, break, business, convert, config, description, else, error, event, extension, framework, isolate, landscape, required, response, review, skill, service, variant
rule: the base carries the full word, never an abbreviation
why: an abbreviation is a consonant skeleton of a longer word, and the embedding reads the short one even when the mark says otherwise. 40 were removed in one pass; 1258 spec occurrences followed, in code position only
check: master: no consonant-subsequence alias inside a concept

wrong: *-> syntree - syntax tree: explicit expectation of the following code
right: (removed)
rule: a concept with no mark and no use is not a concept
why: 0 spec occurrences, no mark in the table. It was an idea parked in the master, where it looked like vocabulary

wrong: *-> temp - weight, temperature, degrees, floating point
right: *-> creative, temp - executor freedom scale 0-100; NOT weight (that is layout); NOT degrees (that is physics)
rule: one description, one concept
why: the description named four meanings, one of which pointed at weight - a different, live concept used 4 times as layout weight="stretch". temp and creative were both 0-use, so the merge cost nothing

wrong: *-> target - target, result
right: *-> target - direct logical indication of a goal: names the entity the task aims at, and nothing else. NOT a result. NOT goal: goal is the marker that the end is here
rule: one description, one concept, and say what it is not
why: 'target, result' was two meanings in one phrase. Both explicit NOTs are load-bearing: the embedding pulls target toward 'result achieved', and toward the goal marker that already exists in the base
check: master: target description names one concept

wrong: environment = the system, the OS
right: environment, env = the variable section (PATH, HOME, ...); os, platform = the target system
rule: the dictionary overrides the embedding, it does not describe it
why: the embedding of 'environment' goes to OS on its own. That is exactly why the base has to say otherwise in words the model cannot argue with
check: master: environment and os are separate concepts

wrong: except = excluding (the embedding)
right: except removed; exception = ERROR AS CONTEXT, the error carried as state
rule: a word whose embedding is louder than the mark must leave the base
why: except means exclusion to every model, and the base was redefining it as error capture. Removing the word is stronger than documenting it

wrong: in as a dictionary word
right: in opens 9 other concepts as a prefix: incld, incr, index, infra, inp, insert, instanceof, instr, nvariant
rule: a short word that opens many others is a context-loss hazard
why: even with include gone, a fragment ending in `in` completes to any of nine. The glyph layer is immune; the text layer is not, and the text layer is what the base is read from

wrong: act
right: action
rule: a word whose embedding fans out to several unrelated senses must be the full one
why: action, activity, actor, and 'Act 1 in an opera'. 997 code occurrences rewritten; the syntax changed from act= to action=, which is visible in every spec

wrong: architect
right: arc
rule: a homophone in the embedding loses to a short unambiguous mark
why: architecture is fine but 'architect' drags in ark, and a model asked to pick a name for a software concept will not reliably pick the one you want. The description already used arc:coroutine - the word was already there
check: master: architect absent, arc present with U+2571

wrong: import is read as in + port
right: import = import library, an actual linked artifact. NOT the in operator, NOT in+out: this is ONE word
rule: state the false readings that the spelling invites
why: inc and port are not in the base, so the tokenizer cannot split it - but a reader can, and in/out are both live operators
check: master: import has no synonyms and names its false readings

wrong: ... in an action scope is spread notation
right: same text, but the base says it is not a name and never compiles
rule: notation and vocabulary are different things and must be marked apart
why: the compiler left it as text either way; the base had been claiming otherwise

wrong: set(radius of theme 15)
right: theme:radius:set(15)
rule: an action scope states the owner with obj:prop, never with a preposition
why: 'of' is the cheap continuation: it carries no anchor, so the reader has to infer which side owns the property. The object was taken from the declaration, not from the English

wrong: load(theme from mapping)
right: load(mapping:theme)
rule: from reverses like of: the thing comes out of the container
why: two occurrences in one spec. The container leads, because that is what the later part of the sentence names

wrong: split(mapping by group)
right: split(mapping:group)
rule: by does NOT reverse: it names the criterion, not the owner
why: the one preposition where the mechanical fold is wrong. Splitting A by B keeps A as the subject

wrong: add(par to nav "view")
right: add(nav:par, "view")
rule: to reverses: A is added to B, so B is the object
why: 21 English relation words in one spec, of which 18 were of and only to/from/by needed a per-line decision

wrong: check(hex:num of theme) == 13
right: check(theme:hex:num) == 13
rule: in a chain the owner leads, then the group, then the property
why: the naive fold gives hex:theme:num, which reads as the theme of hex. The group belongs in the middle

wrong: for(var i=0; i<5; i=incr(1))
right: for(var:i=0:i<5:i=incr(1))
rule: inheritance is explicit, spelled with a colon, everywhere including clause lists
why: a space in a chain is implicit inheritance and it drifts. The semicolon is a context cut and is reserved for that
check: no space inheritance in any code line

wrong: &-> abstract:prop:id="theme"->frm:"theme"
right: &-> abstract:prop:id="theme"->frm:prop
rule: the right side of -> in a declaration is a placement chain, not a pin assignment
why: frm:prop means a prop placed on frm. Spelling it frm:"theme" asserts a field the validator then has to treat as undeclared
check: no quoted self-bind in a declaration chain

wrong: set(frm:font "Arial")
right: frm:font:set("Arial")
rule: a setter is a vector anchored at the end of a path, not a call with arguments
why: two words side by side say nothing about which is the value. The path names the object and :set is applied there, so the chain keeps its meaning. A comma form (set(frm:font,"Arial")) flattens it and was rejected
gate: none - no check sees inside an action scope

wrong: set(view:theme)
right: view:theme:set()
rule: an empty argument is inheritance, not an assignment
why: bind_theme propagates the ambient theme down the tree. A comma there would promise a value that is not given

wrong: show(view)
right: action=show(view)
rule: a verb that reads as an order must be marked as a mapping
why: bare show(left) is an imperative to a person and a cheap continuation to a model. The spec had 20 bare and 3 marked - one word, two forms, the same defect the dictionary spent the day removing
gate: none - no check sees inside an action scope

wrong: &-> abstract:prop:id="tab"->frm:"tab"
right: &-> abstract:item:id="tab_view"->frm:type="tab_view"
rule: fix the category before the name
why: tab is created, added to, closed and shown - it is an element that carries pins, not a property. I saw the collision with the table concept and went looking for a name that would fit, instead of asking what the thing is. tab_view removes the collision because the thing is named for what it is

wrong: ->tab:num:set(par)
right: ->tab_view:num:set(par)
rule: a word in command position must be a declared command
why: RE_CMD_WORD takes any word after -> as a command. The vector form puts the owner first, so an undeclared owner becomes an unknown command. Declaring it as an item fixed two errors that had nothing to do with the change that surfaced them

wrong: U+279E target
right: U+233E target
rule: a round-tipped arrow reads as call-and-return, not as the point being aimed at
why: the mark is what the model reads. U+279E was visually close to -> as well, so a reader saw a relation where the word meant a destination

wrong: min = U+25BE, max = U+25B4
right: min = U+230A, max = U+230B
rule: a mark must not look like a different operator
why: U+25BE/U+25B4 are small triangles, already reading as down/up arrows in a language that has up and down

wrong: 15 action= strings carrying of/from/by/to/in after the code was fixed
right: prose restated in the language's own terms, or the check extended to prose
rule: prose is the first thing a model reads, so it is not documentation - it is input
why: ENGLISH reported 0 because it scans code position only. The prose still said 'split mapping by group' after the code said split(mapping:group), so the spec was teaching a form that no longer existed

wrong: add_tab inlines tab:name:set(par)
right: add_tab calls run(set_tab_name)
rule: one function per operation, named
why: set_tab_name already existed and did exactly that. Two sources of truth for one operation, which is the duplication the dictionary work was removing everywhere else

wrong: a script printed ZAPISANO and changed nothing
right: verify by reading the file, not the tool's report
rule: an instrument's report is a claim; the file is the fact
why: set_comma.py applied and reported success, and there were zero commas in the file. I checked only the 10 sites I expected to stay unchanged and concluded it had worked. Three tools said 'done' this session and two of them lied
check: counted in the file after every apply
gate: none - this is a habit, not a check

wrong: printing a reconstructed 'before' instead of the matched text
right: print m.group(0)
rule: a pretty before hides a no-op
why: the plan showed set(view:name, "VibeDSL IDE") with a comma that was not in the file, which is why the no-op in tool-01 looked successful

wrong: a pattern whose halves live on opposite sides of a segment edge
right: do not match show( when show is a code run and ( opens a keep run
rule: quoted payload is never rewritten, so code and payload live in different chunks - a regex cannot span the seam
why: hit this three times in one session: show(, then tab before a colon, then a lookahead. Each looked like the target was simply absent

wrong: a lookahead excluding a real value: (?!none\b)
right: empty forms have nothing after the pin, so no lookahead is needed
rule: a guard written to skip an empty case can swallow a legitimate one
why: set(nav:content none) - setting the nav to the none marker - was silently skipped. The guard was meant for set(view:theme), which has no trailing token at all

wrong: "the word platform is not in the base at all"
right: platform is already an alias of os
rule: search for a word, then read the lines that come back
why: I searched for lines STARTING with platform and concluded it was absent, then reported that as a finding. It was there as the second name of os

wrong: "except is removed, the trap is closed"
right: except was still in the base; only excpt had gone
rule: do not report a change before reading the file
why: I had written "except": None in the rename map meaning 'already handled by hand', and had not handled it. The claim came from the intention, not the state

wrong: "target is a platform binding in the base"
right: its description reads 'target, result' - nothing about platforms
rule: do not carry a conclusion across from a neighbouring word
why: I bundled os/platform/targ and applied to all three a claim I had only checked for the first. platform turned out to be an alias of os, not of target

wrong: "19 concepts without a mark are candidates for a mark or deletion"
right: 19 before, 19 after, byte-identical list
rule: what you did not create and did not break is not yours
why: I checked one of them against a backup and generalised to all nineteen, then proposed work nobody asked for. The base is shared; if every pass tidies what it finds, it becomes a cleaning rota instead of a workshop

wrong: 19 concepts reported as having no mark, read as cleanup candidates
right: left alone; reported as reference state
rule: a reader with the dictionary in context is not the reader the base is written for
why: same failure as dict-05, at larger scale: familiar state stops looking like state

wrong: a trailing comma in a head
right: no trailing comma
rule: cosmetic means invisible to me, not to a fresh reader
why: this was the correction that produced the DICT f rule: cosmetic is a statement about my context, not about the data

wrong: id and param may repeat in one spec - a param belongs to its function, so param=file twice is harmless
right: a word bound twice is a VECTOR on that word; id and param are one namespace and each name is bound once per spec
rule: one word, one binding, one meaning, per spec
why: I found five real vectors in PY_IDE/window.vibe - file, param x3, size, name - and then relaxed the check that found them, on the grounds that a param is function-local. That reasoning is exactly the error: the repetition IS the defect, whether or not each function means something different by it. Softening a check because a finding looks harmless is how a finding stops being reported, and the finding was right.

wrong: a spec may declare id="theme" because in this spec theme is a prop
right: a spec may not claim a name the base already explains; it uses the base word as it is
rule: the base owns the word, a spec owns the placement
why: 27 of 50 declarations in window.vibe did this - view, theme, text, frm, left and 23 more, the same collision as goal and col. It also cost the compiler: a locally claimed name has to be spared from compiling, so show(theme) stopped being a mark until the claim was removed. The name was never the spec's to take.

wrong: a command written as check(x) never compiles, because everything inside () is protected
right: () and [] are transparent - a word inside them is a word - and {} stays protected because a brace block is a free-form custom block
rule: quotes and {} protect; () and [] do not
why: I fixed a non-canonical != by writing !(check(x) == none), which moved check inside a paren and stopped it compiling - a fix for one word on a line broke a working word on the same line, and the report still said 9 so it looked finished. The paren was never meant to hide a command.

wrong: the compile report says one line has a non-canonical !=
right: it deduplicates: one message stood for ten occurrences, and both had to be found by grepping
rule: a deduplicated report counts kinds, not places
why: scop= and != were reported as one line each. scop= was one. != was ten. Reading the count instead of grepping would have left nine of them, and I only found them because the number felt too small.

wrong: protecting locally declared names from compiling is how paren transparency can be added safely
right: the protection was a symptom - the spec had claimed 27 names from the base, and removing the claims removed the need for the exception
rule: fix the collision, do not shield from it
why: local_names() covered up exactly what binding-02 describes. Two mechanisms, one cause, and the covering one is what would have kept the cause alive.

wrong: rename a bound word across the whole action string
right: a parameter name and a pin name are different things that happen to share a word; renaming one must not touch the other
rule: rename the binding, not the vocabulary
why: set_tab_name has param=name and writes tab_view:name:set(par). Replacing the word name also rewrote the PIN path to tab_view:name_tab:set(par), and the checker caught it as an undeclared field on tab_view. Two bindings of one word, renamed as if they were one, is how a safe rename becomes a new defect. The same pass also bound fill_editor to content while line 96 already held content - a vector I created while removing vectors.

wrong: derive what to protect from the same text the compiler rewrites
right: local_names() read id= followed by a quote, and = compiles to U+2A72, so a second pass saw an empty set and compiled everything the first pass had shielded
rule: anything the compiler rewrites cannot be used to describe its own input
why: this is what broke idempotence, and the symptom pointed somewhere else entirely: the glyph legend grew 62 to 123, so I blamed the legend. The extra glyphs were -, to, is, :, child, line - header marks - which is the proof that pass two was compiling words pass one had protected. The fix is one character class. The diagnosis took three wrong turns: I read the count instead of diffing the legends, I blamed glyphs_used where a dead duplicated if had looked guilty, and I was about to rewrite the legend. Diff the two outputs and the extra marks are the witness; the count alone says nothing about where they came from.
